name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,770

clue.text: Cross? Violently angry, I will get to snapping bones, possibly (1-6)

indicators.note: something treated violently is thrown about, so the letters of ANGRY I land in a new order

blocks.note: a cross is the letter X

annotation.surface: Someone asks if you are cross, and the reply is that they are so furious they will soon be breaking bones.
annotation.walkthrough: The opening question mark makes 'Cross?' look like a question about mood; it is the letter X. 'Snapping' is photographing, not breaking, which the 'possibly' flags.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example with a pun: 'snap' is slang for taking a photograph, so photographing bones with X-rays is one way of snapping them.

clue.text: Console youngster, shortly covered in kisses (4)

indicators.note: said shortly, a word is cut short, so BOY loses its last letter
something covered in kisses has them on both sides, so BO sits between the two Xs

blocks.note: X is a kiss; two of them

annotation.surface: An adult comforts a child by smothering them in kisses.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Console' reads as a verb, to comfort, in the surface; it is the noun, a games console.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Microsoft's games machine is one kind of console, the box that plugs into a television.

clue.text: Island's unnamed lizard detailed by active conservationists (7)

indicators.note: N is the abbreviation for name, so un-named means the lizard loses its N
read as de-tailed: the lizard's tail, its last letter, is cut off
by means beside, so the lizard stands next to the conservationists

blocks.note: the National Trust, the British heritage and conservation charity
IGUANA without its N and without its final A

annotation.surface: An island's nameless lizard is being described in detail by busy conservation workers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Detailed' looks like 'described closely'; read it as de-tailed. 'Unnamed' works the same way, removing N for name.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this Caribbean country, home of St John's, is one of many islands.

clue.text: Characteristic style of Oscar Wilde I am occasionally to cover (5)

indicators.note: something done occasionally happens only now and then, so only every other letter is taken
to cover something is to go over and around it, so the alternate letters wrap round the O

blocks.note: second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of WILDEIAM
Oscar is O in the phonetic alphabet

annotation.surface: A remark about Oscar Wilde's distinctive way of writing, as if Wilde were speaking.
annotation.walkthrough: Oscar and Wilde go together so naturally that the solver reads them as one name; they are split, Oscar giving O and Wilde starting the letter run.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an idiom can mean the distinctive manner of an artist or school, a characteristic style.

clue.text: Comes through, in adversity - takes balls (4,4)

blocks.note: in cricket an over is six balls bowled

annotation.surface: Someone survives a bad time, and it takes courage ('balls') to do it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Balls' reads as slang for nerve; here it is the cricket over, six deliveries in a row.
annotation.definitionFit: A phrasal-verb synonym: recovering from an illness or setback is coming through it, and 'in adversity' names the kind of thing overcome.

clue.text: Tell's apple, brief hazard for lad's crown (7)

indicators.note: something brief is cut short, so RISK loses its last letter
for means in place of, so RIS stands where the L was

blocks.note: the top letter of LAD, which RIS replaces

annotation.surface: William Tell shooting an apple off his son's head, a danger to the boy's crown.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is the William Tell legend, so 'Tell' looks like a name; it is the verb, and the apple is just letters to edit.
annotation.definitionFit: A formal synonym: to apprise is to inform, from the French 'appris', learned, so telling someone news fits.

clue.text: Laid odds (only evens) against increases (4,2)

indicators.note: evens are the even-numbered positions, so only letters two, four, six and eight are kept

blocks.note: second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of LAIDODDS
against = to, as in 'back to the wall'

annotation.surface: A bookmaker offered odds, all at evens, against something happening.
annotation.walkthrough: The betting words 'odds' and 'evens' look like racing talk; 'evens' is the instruction to keep even-numbered letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A phrasal-verb synonym: to add to a pile or a problem is to make it bigger, to increase it.

clue.text: Penniless, devout old character rising within (9)

indicators.note: in a down clue, a word rising reads from bottom to top, so RUNE turns round
within means inside, so the upturned rune goes inside PIOUS

blocks.note: a rune is a letter of an old alphabet

annotation.surface: A poor, devout figure from long ago who rises up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Character' reads as a person; it is a letter, the rune.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: penury is poverty, so being penurious means lacking money.

clue.text: Innocent lass, German girl, gets naked on leaving Germany (7)

indicators.note: to leave is to go away, so D for Germany departs from NUDE

blocks.note: Inge is a German girl's name
D is the international vehicle code for Germany; it is removed

annotation.surface: An innocent German girl strips once she has left her country.
annotation.walkthrough: D for Germany comes from Deutschland, as on car stickers.
annotation.definitionFit: A theatre term: the ingenue is the stock role of an innocent, unworldly young woman.

clue.text: Nosh with setters followed by hanky-panky around southern county (4,6)

indicators.note: with means alongside, so US joins EATS
followed by means coming after, so SEX goes after them
around means surrounding, so EATS is wrapped round the S

blocks.note: nosh and eats are both slang for food
hanky-panky is a coy word for sex

annotation.surface: A cosy, racy picture of food, company and flirting in the south of England.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Southern' looks like part of the definition, but it supplies the S inside EATS.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the county on England's south coast containing Brighton and Hastings is one county among many.

clue.text: Bamboozled and unmasked idiot breaking in (9)

indicators.note: a burglar breaking in gets inside, so TWIT forces its way into OUTED

blocks.note: to be outed is to be exposed

annotation.surface: A fool is caught breaking into a house and has his mask pulled off, baffled.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Breaking in' belongs to the burglary picture, which hides that it is the instruction to put one word inside another.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past tense: being beaten by someone cleverer leaves you bamboozled, fooled.

clue.text: Hot drink with cinnamon, e.g., using only a bit (5)

indicators.note: using only a bit of something means taking a small piece of it, so the answer is a stretch of the letters

annotation.surface: A recipe note: warm drink with cinnamon, just a pinch.
annotation.walkthrough: The recipe surface makes 'only a bit' sound like a quantity of spice; it is telling you the answer is a small part of the words.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: negus, named after Colonel Francis Negus, is warm port or sherry with sugar and spice, a hot drink.

clue.text: Willing for those neglected originally to be represented in series (4,2,7)

indicators.note: originally means at the start, so only the first letter of 'neglected' is used
re-presented means presented again in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: A call for neglected groups to get fair representation on television.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is about diversity on screen; 'represented' is the anagram instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the HBO fantasy drama is a television series.

clue.text: On board a cabin cruiser, each passenger heads to topside (10)

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so each word gives its initial
in a down clue the top side is above, so these letters sit on top of TABLE

blocks.note: a board is a table, as in 'bed and board'

annotation.surface: Passengers on a cabin cruiser all go up on deck.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On board' reads as one nautical phrase; split it, and 'On' alone is the definition while 'board' is TABLE.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'that's not on' means it is not acceptable, so 'on' alone means acceptable.

clue.text: It nips, it uses teeth heartlessly, it's more snappy (8)

indicators.note: without a heart means without the middle, so BITER loses its central T

blocks.note: a crab nips with its claws
a biter; its middle T goes

annotation.surface: A description of some fierce creature that nips and bites and is getting more irritable.
annotation.walkthrough: Each 'it' starts a new piece; the repetition makes the clue read like one animal being described.
annotation.definitionFit: A comparative synonym: crabby means irritable, so crabbier is quicker to snap at people, matching the crab that nips.

clue.text: Girl group first succeeded with brightly-coloured headgear (9)

indicators.note: first means coming before, so the group goes ahead of the girl

annotation.surface: A girl group's first hit came wearing colourful headscarves.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Girl group' reads as one pop phrase; it splits into the girl and the group, and 'first' puts the group in front.
annotation.definitionFit: A plural definition by description: these patterned cotton scarves are knotted round the head, so they count as headgear.

clue.text: They wear shorts and pants (6)

blocks.note: boxer shorts, a style of men's underpants

annotation.surface: A plain statement that some people wear shorts and pants.
annotation.walkthrough: In British English pants are underpants. The clue reads as one list of clothes, but it holds two separate definitions.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: fighters in the ring wear shorts, and boxer shorts are a loose style of underpants, called pants in Britain.

clue.text: Fault in bit of cinematography rectified - version ready for release (5,3)

indicators.note: a bit of a word is a small piece of it, here its first letter
something rectified is put right, so the letters are set in a new, correct order

annotation.surface: A flaw in some camera work is fixed so the film can go out.
annotation.walkthrough: The film-making surface fits the answer exactly, so the definition hides in plain sight.
annotation.definitionFit: A film-industry term: the last edit a director approves is the one sent out to cinemas, the version ready for release.

clue.text: Ultimately lose knight to chess champ's closing moves (6)

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of 'lose' is used

blocks.note: N is the chess notation for a knight

annotation.surface: A chess champion loses a knight in the endgame.
annotation.walkthrough: 'To' just joins the pieces in order. The chess surface is apt: the ending is the last phase of a game.
annotation.definitionFit: A chess term: the last phase of a game, when few pieces remain, is called the ending or endgame.

clue.text: Conned king for power, medal and lordly title (7)

indicators.note: for means in exchange for, so K goes in where P was

blocks.note: K is the king, as in chess
the Order of Merit, a British honour

annotation.surface: A king was tricked into swapping power for honours and titles.
annotation.walkthrough: 'King for power' reads as a trade; it is the instruction to put K where P was.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the rank held by a duke, the highest hereditary title below prince, is a lordly title.

clue.text: Rapidly recruiting US taxmen for high-level domain? (8)

indicators.note: to recruit is to take people in, so APACE takes the taxmen inside it

annotation.surface: A US tax agency hurriedly hiring for a senior post.
annotation.walkthrough: 'High-level' sounds like seniority in a job; the question mark flags that it means literally high up in the sky.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic definition by description: the sky above a country is territory it controls, a domain that is literally high up.

clue.text: Yankee President cycling over to NATO, say (7)

indicators.note: a cycle goes round and round, so letters move from the front round to the back

blocks.note: Yankee is Y in the phonetic alphabet

annotation.surface: An American president turns up at a NATO meeting.
annotation.walkthrough: The first two letters of YMACRON go round to the end. 'Yankee President' reads as one American; they are two pieces, and the president is French.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: NATO is built from the initials of North Atlantic Treaty Organization and spoken as a word.

clue.text: Rabble-rousing leader has women's group round the twist (6)

indicators.note: a leader goes at the front, so this takes the first letter of rabble-rousing
to have something is to hold it, so the R holds WI around it
round means surrounding, so WI is placed on either side of the R

blocks.note: the Women's Institute, a British community organisation for women

annotation.surface: A demagogue brings a women's group to the brink of madness.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Round the twist' is British slang for crazy, so the phrase reads as one idea; 'the' is letters and 'twist' is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: squirming about in pain means twisting the body.

clue.text: Try to pot one red, initially maintaining break, finally switching to the rest (4,1,8)

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the first letter of red is used
to maintain is to hold, so A and R hold BREATHE between them
the final letter of BREAK is switched, swapped out for THE

blocks.note: in snooker, to take a ball is to pot it
its final K is replaced by THE

annotation.surface: A snooker player lines up a red and builds a break, then reaches for the rest.
annotation.walkthrough: Snooker words are everywhere: break, red, pot and the rest (a cue support). 'The' supplies letters for the swap, and 'rest' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: stopping briefly to recover your breath means resting, as a snooker player might between frames.

clue.text: Drinks cuppa, left unfinished in hurry (5)

indicators.note: something left unfinished lacks its end, so TEA loses its final letter

blocks.note: to have a drink is to drink it
a cuppa is a cup of tea; its A is dropped

annotation.surface: Someone gulps a cup of tea and leaves it half drunk in a rush.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like the direction L; with 'unfinished' it means the tea is left incomplete.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain noun synonym: excess speed, the rush of someone late, is hurry; 'in haste' and 'in a hurry' match.

clue.text: I think it's a book (4)

blocks.note: a phrase meaning 'in my view', written as two short words

annotation.surface: Someone guessing what an object is: a book, they think.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I think' reads as hedging; run together, 'to me' (as in 'to me, it's a book') gives the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: 'to me' means in my opinion, and closed up it is a large heavy volume, a kind of book.

clue.text: Hunter maybe returning horned ibex hides (5)

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so the hidden letters read backwards
to hide something is to conceal it, so the answer is concealed in the words

annotation.surface: A hunter coming back with the skin of a horned mountain goat.
annotation.walkthrough: The hunting scene makes 'Hunter' a job; it is a first name, and 'hides' is a verb, not animal skins.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Hunter is the first name of Joe Biden's son, so a Biden is what Hunter is.

clue.text: Fat monk loves eats (5,4)

blocks.note: Friar Tuck, the stout friar of the Robin Hood stories

annotation.surface: A greedy monk adores his food.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Eats' looks like a noun (food), the thing the monk loves; it is the verb and the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A phrasal-verb synonym: to tuck into a meal is to eat it with gusto.

clue.text: Scattered SAS men finally strike as one (2,5)

indicators.note: things scattered are strewn about, so the letters land in a new order
finally means at the end, so only the last letter of strike is used

annotation.surface: Special forces soldiers, spread out, attack together.
annotation.walkthrough: The SAS is the British Army's special forces regiment. 'Strike' reads as the attack; only its last letter is used.
annotation.definitionFit: A French phrase used in English: 'in a mass', all together, so acting as one body.

clue.text: The Queen Mother entered hot springs (7)

indicators.note: to enter is to go inside, so ER and MA go inside THE

blocks.note: the word itself, opened up to take the others

annotation.surface: The Queen Mother bathing in hot springs.
annotation.walkthrough: The royal title reads as one person, the late Queen Mother; the three words work separately. ER for a queen dates from Elizabeth II's reign.
annotation.definitionFit: A Latin plural: Roman public baths fed by warm water were thermae, from the Greek for heat, hence hot springs.
